item.text: I’ve got the reference path and the source layout. The fastest route here is to lean heavily on the upstream tests for the listed behavior areas, then fill in edge cases by probing the binary where the tests are silent.

The listed commands are mostly streaming CSV transforms, so I’m going to implement a compact local CSV engine around Python’s stdlib `csv`, plus just enough selection/range parsing to match xsv’s command grammar. Next I’m reading the command docs and tests in parallel.

Selection syntax is the trickiest little knot so far: names, indexes, reverse ranges, open ranges, inversion, and duplicate headers. I’m carrying that over almost literally, because lots of other commands reuse it.

I’m at the edit point now. I’m going to add a self-contained Python CLI plus a compile script that removes any stale higher-priority wrapper and creates a Windows-friendly `executable.cmd` in this workspace.

The first version is in place. I’m compiling the entrypoint and then I’ll start differential checks against the official executable, beginning with the Rust unit-test examples and then a few behavior probes for formatting details.

item.text: The failures are all the same species: CSV rows written through Python’s text stdout are becoming Windows CRLF, while the Rust binary emits LF unless `fmt --crlf` is requested. I’m switching CSV stdout writes to an in-memory buffer and then writing raw bytes, so the line endings stay exact.
Line ending fix is in. I’m re-running the same representative set, this time with a cleaner byte comparison so the report is less noisy.

item.text: The wider pass found real issues, not just cosmetics: frequency has to keep an empty value distinct from the literal string `(NULL)` until output time, and stats needs Rust-like numeric display instead of Python’s floaty `5.0` for integer columns. I’m tightening those now, plus matching the slice error’s “header first, then fail” behavior.
One subtle correction: Rust writes the header before validating the slice range, so even the error case can have stdout. I’m mirroring that ordering explicitly.
Those fixes are in. I’m rechecking the failing cases and using a quoted empty field for stats too, which matches how the Rust tests create a one-column NULL row.

item.text: Two more details surfaced: xsv’s stats min/max ignores NULLs even when NULLs count toward mean/stddev, and its tie order in frequency keeps the real empty value ahead of ordinary values while the literal `(NULL)` sorts later. I’m matching those observed rules and switching stddev to the same one-pass population algorithm the Rust stats crate uses.
The tie and numeric-stat fixes are in; I’m doing another byte pass over those focused cases, then I’ll run a final larger sweep.
